title: Administrative Work - Canadian SR&ED Tax Credit Glossary
description: Learn why clerical and Administrative Work is generally excluded from direct R&D claims in our Canadian SR&ED tax credit glossary.
summary: Administrative work in claims under Canada's federal SR&ED tax incentive program is treated differently by calculation method: under the proxy method, administrative and other support wages are not claimed separately because the 55% prescribed proxy amount covers them, while under the traditional method, directly attributable administrative wages are claimed as overhead under Income Tax Regulations paragraph 2900(2)(c).

body.text: Administrative work in claims under Canada's federal SR&ED tax incentive program is treated differently by calculation method: under the proxy method, administrative and other support wages are not claimed separately because the 55% prescribed proxy amount covers them, while under the traditional method, directly attributable administrative wages are claimed as overhead under Income Tax Regulations paragraph 2900(2)(c).

This report delivers a comprehensive legal, technical, and financial audit of the research and development (R&D) tax incentive framework, direct innovation funding interactions, provincial and territorial regimes, compliance procedures, and judicial precedents of Canada as of November 2026.

As of November 2026, Canada's Scientific Research and Experimental Development (SR&ED) Tax Incentive Program operates under its largest legislative expansion in over a decade following the enactment of Bill C-15, which introduced the November 4, 2025 federal budget measures and received Royal Assent on March 26, 2026. Retroactive to taxation years beginning after December 15, 2024, Bill C-15 doubled the maximum annual expenditure limit for the enhanced 35% SR&ED investment tax credit (ITC) from $3,000,000 to $6,000,000 (superseding an interim $4,500,000 proposal from late 2024), widened the prior-year taxable capital phase-out range from $10 million–$50 million to $15 million–$75 million, extended the enhanced 35% ITC to Eligible Canadian Public Corporations (ECPCs), permitted Canadian-controlled private corporations (CCPCs) to elect a three-year average gross revenue phase-out instead of taxable capital, and restored SR&ED deductions and ITCs for capital expenditures and equipment lease costs incurred after December 15, 2024. Operationally, on April 1, 2026, the CRA launched an optional pre-claim approval process providing up-front technical eligibility determinations within eight weeks and cutting post-filing expenditure review service targets from 180 days to 90 days. Provincially, Quebec abolished six legacy R&D tax credits for taxation years beginning after March 25, 2025, consolidating them into the refundable 30% / 20% Tax Credit for Research, Innovation and Commercialization (CRIC), which Revenu Québec designates the Tax Credit for R&D, Innovation and Pre-Commercialization, whereas federally—despite 2024 consultations and 2025 election platform pledges—Ottawa has not enacted a federal "patent box" regime as of November 2026.
1. Legislative Architecture and the 2024–2026 Statutory Overhaul
1.1 Statutory Foundations in the Income Tax Act and Income Tax Regulations

Canada's federal R&D tax incentive system is codified in Section 37, Section 127, Section 127.1, and Subsection 248(1) of the federal Income Tax Act, together with Section 2900 of the Income Tax Regulations. Rather than operating as a competitive or discretionary grant envelope, the SR&ED program is a statutory entitlement integrated into self-assessed income tax filings: any taxpayer carrying on a business in Canada whose technical activities meet the legal definition of SR&ED in subsection 248(1) and who submits prescribed forms containing all prescribed information on or before the statutory SR&ED reporting deadline is entitled to two complementary incentives. First, the claimant aggregates allowable current and post-December 15, 2024 capital SR&ED outlays into a cumulative pool of deductible SR&ED expenditures under subsection 37(1) to reduce net business income in the current or future taxation years. Second, the claimant earns an SR&ED investment tax credit under subsections 127(5) and 127(9) that offsets Part I federal tax payable and, for eligible claimants under section 127.1, yields a direct cash refund.

Every rule governing eligible labour, overhead methodologies, corporate association, non-arm's length transfers, government assistance deductions, property recapture, filing deadlines, and civil penalties maps to specific provisions of the Income Tax Act and Income Tax Regulations, in the table below.

body.text: 1.2 Chronology of Enactment: From the 2024 Fall Economic Statement to Bill C-15

A frequent source of error in unverified Canadian tax commentary written between late 2024 and early 2026 is confusing initial legislative proposals from the 2024 Fall Economic Statement with the expanded statutory thresholds ultimately enacted into law.

items: 2024 Fall Economic Statement and 2025 Draft Legislation: Department of Finance Canada initially proposed—for taxation years beginning after December 15, 2024—increasing the annual expenditure limit for the 35% enhanced SR&ED ITC from $3,000,000 to $4,500,000, raising the prior-year taxable capital phase-out thresholds from $10 million–$50 million to $15 million–$75 million, extending the 35% enhanced ITC to Eligible Canadian Public Corporations, allowing CCPCs to elect a gross-revenue phase-out, and restoring capital expenditure and lease eligibility for outlays after December 15, 2024.

November 4, 2025 Federal Budget (Budget 2025): In its November 4, 2025 federal budget, the Government of Canada superseded the interim $4,500,000 proposal and further increased the annual enhanced expenditure limit to $6,000,000—doubling the pre-reform $3,000,000 threshold—retroactive to taxation years beginning after December 15, 2024. Budget 2025 concurrently introduced administrative reforms scheduled for April 1, 2026, including an elective pre-claim approval mechanism, expanded artificial intelligence risk-scoring for low-risk claims, and targeted consultations on Form T661.

March 26, 2026 Royal Assent of Bill C-15: Parliament enacted the Budget 2025 SR&ED legislative package via Bill C-15, which received Royal Assent on March 26, 2026 (making the measures enacted for U.S. GAAP financial reporting purposes on March 26, 2026).

body.text: 2. Federal SR&ED Tax Incentive Rates, Thresholds, Refundability, and Carryovers
2.1 Dual-Mechanism Structure: Subsection 37(1) Pool Deduction vs. Section 127 Investment Tax Credit

The federal SR&ED program delivers tax relief through two distinct statutory calculations. First, under subsection 37(1), allowable current SR&ED expenditures (paragraph 37(1)(a)) and—for depreciable property acquired and available for use after December 15, 2024—allowable SR&ED capital expenditures (paragraph 37(1)(b)), reduced by government and non-government assistance (paragraph 37(1)(d)), enter a cumulative pool of deductible SR&ED expenditures. Claimants may deduct pool balances against current-year business income or retain unclaimed SR&ED expenditures in the pool for deduction in future taxation years. Crucially, neither the notional Prescribed Proxy Amount (PPA) calculated under the proxy method nor the capital cost of Shared-Use Equipment (SUE) enters the subsection 37(1) deductible pool; SUE must instead be depreciated under standard Capital Cost Allowance (CCA) rules on Schedule T2SCH8, and any SR&ED ITC earned on SUE reduces the Undepreciated Capital Cost (UCC) of the applicable CCA class in the following taxation year.

Second, under subsections 127(5) and 127(9) and section 127.1, the claimant earns an SR&ED Investment Tax Credit (ITC) equal to either 35% (the enhanced rate, comprising the 15% basic rate plus a 20% enhancement) or 15% (the basic rate) of the excess of its year-end SR&ED qualified expenditure pool over any provincial super-allowance benefit amounts.
2.2 Enhanced 35% vs. Basic 15% Credit Rates and Claimant Categories

Entitlement to the enhanced 35% rate versus the basic 15% rate depends on corporate status and taxation-year start date. Canadian-controlled private corporations (CCPCs) defined under subsection 125(7) earn the enhanced 35% ITC on qualified SR&ED expenditures up to their annual expenditure limit—$3,000,000 for taxation years beginning before December 16, 2024 (up to $1,050,000 in enhanced credits) and $6,000,000 for taxation years beginning after December 15, 2024 (up to $2,100,000 in enhanced credits)—and earn the basic 15% ITC on qualified expenditures above that limit.

For taxation years beginning after December 15, 2024, Bill C-15 extended the enhanced 35% ITC up to the $6,000,000 expenditure limit to Eligible Canadian Public Corporations (ECPCs) defined under subsection 127(9), which previously earned only the non-refundable 15% rate. To qualify as an ECPC, a corporation must satisfy three cumulative requirements: it must be resident in Canada; it must have a class of shares listed on a designated stock exchange (or have elected, or been designated by the Minister of National Revenue, to be a public corporation); and it must not be controlled, directly or indirectly in any manner whatever, by one or more non-resident persons. Qualified expenditures exceeding an ECPC's expenditure limit earn the 15% basic rate.

All other claimants earn the basic 15% ITC on qualified SR&ED expenditures without an expenditure cap: corporations that are neither CCPCs nor ECPCs (such as foreign-controlled Canadian subsidiaries), sole proprietorships (individuals), partners of a partnership (subsection 127(8)), and beneficiaries of trusts. Under subsection 127(9), however, no SR&ED ITC can be earned on expenditures incurred in the course of earning income from a business if any of the claimant's income from that business is exempt from Part I tax—excluding Crown corporations (other than Prescribed Federal Crown Corporations) and tax-exempt non-profit corporations from earning ITCs.
2.3 Expenditure Limit Phase-Out Mechanics: Taxable Capital vs. Elective Gross Revenue Method

For taxation years beginning before December 16, 2024, a CCPC's $3,000,000 expenditure limit began decreasing once the prior-year taxable capital employed in Canada (sections 181.2, 181.3, and 181.4) of the CCPC and its associated corporations reached $10,000,000, phasing out linearly to nil at $50,000,000.

For taxation years beginning after December 15, 2024, Bill C-15 raised the phase-out boundaries to $15,000,000 and $75,000,000 (a $60,000,000 phase-out span reducing the $6,000,000 limit by $1 for every $10 above $15,000,000) and established two alternative phase-out methods. Under the Taxable Capital Method (default for CCPCs under subsections 127(10.2) and 127(10.21)), the $6,000,000 expenditure limit phases out between $15,000,000 and $75,000,000 of aggregate prior-year taxable capital employed in Canada across the CCPC and all associated CCPCs: Expenditure Limit = $6,000,000 × ($75,000,000 − Prior-Year Group Taxable Capital) ÷ $60,000,000.

Under the Gross Revenue Method (mandatory for ECPCs under subsections 127(10.6) and 127(10.62), and elective for single CCPCs under subsection 127(10.31) and associated CCPC groups under subsection 127(10.32)), the $6,000,000 expenditure limit begins decreasing once average annual gross revenue over the preceding three fiscal years reaches $15,000,000, reaching nil at $75,000,000 or greater: Expenditure Limit = $6,000,000 × ($75,000,000 − 3-Year Average Annual Group Revenue) ÷ $60,000,000. For ECPCs, annual revenue is determined from the consolidated financial statements (subsection 233.8(1)) of the consolidated group, which shares a single expenditure limit. Where a CCPC belongs to an associated group, all associated CCPCs must jointly elect to use the revenue method, summing financial-statement annual revenue for every current-year group member across the preceding three fiscal years—regardless of whether the corporations were associated throughout that entire three-year window—including each corporation's reasonable share of partnership or trust revenue and allowing reasonable adjustments to eliminate intra-group sales so the group reflects a single economic entity.

Associated CCPCs allocate their shared expenditure limit by filing Schedule T2SCH49 (subsection 127(10.3)), failing which the Minister allocates the limit under subsection 127(10.4). Where a corporation has a short taxation year (fewer than 51 weeks), its expenditure limit is prorated under subsection 127(10.5) (CCPCs) or subsection 127(10.64) (ECPCs) by (Days in Tax Year ÷ 365)—for example, a $3,000,000 allocated share over a 184-day short taxation year from July 1 to December 31, 2027 prorates to $3,000,000 × (184 ÷ 365) = $1,512,329—and special rules govern associated CCPCs with multiple taxation years ending in the same calendar year.

Two practical scenarios published in April 2026 tax advisory guidance by Doane Grant Thornton illustrate the magnitude of these enacted changes. First, consider a CCPC with $45,000,000 of prior-year taxable capital in Canada, $40,000,000 of three-year average gross revenue, $500,000 of prior-year taxable income, and $4,500,000 of current qualified R&D expenditures: under pre-December 16, 2024 law, its expenditure limit shrank to $375,000 ($3M × ($50M − $45M) ÷ $40M), yielding $131,250 of refundable 35% ITCs and $618,750 of non-refundable 15% ITCs ($750,000 total); under Bill C-15, electing the gross revenue method raises its expenditure limit to $3,500,000 ($6M × ($75M − $40M) ÷ $60M), generating $1,225,000 of refundable 35% ITCs plus $150,000 of non-refundable 15% ITCs on the remaining $1,000,000 ($1,375,000 total). Second, an ECPC with $40,000,000 of three-year average consolidated gross revenue and $3,500,000 of current qualified R&D expenditures previously received $0 in refundable credits and $525,000 (15%) in non-refundable ITCs; under Bill C-15, its expenditure limit is $3,500,000, yielding $1,225,000 (35%) in 100% refundable federal tax credits.
2.4 Refundability Rules, Carryover Horizons, and Acquisition-of-Control Restrictions

Under section 127.1, unused current-year SR&ED ITCs are refunded in cash according to strict statutory tiers distinguishing current expenditures from restored capital expenditures. Qualifying CCPCs and ECPCs earn a 100% cash refund on unused 35% enhanced ITCs attributable to current SR&ED expenditures up to their expenditure limit (delivering up to $2,100,000 per year in federal cash refunds on $6,000,000 of current R&D spending). By contrast, where a CCPC or ECPC earns the 35% enhanced ITC on restored capital expenditures (post-December 15, 2024), only 40% of that 35% ITC is refundable (an immediate 14% cash yield), while the remaining 60% is non-refundable. Qualifying CCPCs also receive 40% refundability on basic 15% ITCs earned above their expenditure limit, and unincorporated individuals and eligible trusts receive 40% refundability on their 15% basic ITCs, whereas non-CCPC/non-ECPC corporations receive 0% refundability.

Unused non-refundable SR&ED ITCs may be carried back 3 taxation years and carried forward 20 taxation years to offset federal Part I tax payable. Under section 127, however, a corporate acquisition of control restricts both the carryforward of unused SR&ED ITCs earned before the acquisition of control and the carryback of SR&ED ITCs earned after the acquisition of control.

body.text: 3. Scientific and Technological Eligibility Criteria and Judicial Precedents
3.1 Subsection 248(1) Definition and Eligible Categories of Work

Technical eligibility for federal SR&ED incentives is governed by subsection 248(1) of the Income Tax Act, which defines SR&ED as a "systematic investigation or search that is carried out in a field of science or technology by means of experiment or analysis". Eligible scientific or technological work encompasses three core branches alongside directly related support activities: basic research (work undertaken for the advancement of scientific knowledge with no practical application in view); applied research (work undertaken for the advancement of scientific knowledge with a specific practical application in view); and experimental development (work undertaken for the purpose of achieving technological advancement to create new materials, products, devices, or processes, or to improve existing ones, including incremental improvements). Directly commensurate support activities that assist the prosecution of eligible basic research, applied research, or experimental development also qualify, whereas commercial production (including passing software or manufactured goods into consumer markets or running excess production batches) and routine engineering or standard procedures are strictly excluded from SR&ED.
3.2 Foundational Jurisprudence: The Northwest Hydraulic Five-Question Test

Although the CRA publishes administrative guidance—most notably the Guidelines on the eligibility of work for scientific research and experimental development (SR&ED) tax incentives issued on August 13, 2021—Canadian courts evaluate every disputed SR&ED appeal against the binding five-question test established by Justice Donald Bowman in Northwest Hydraulic Consultants Ltd. v. The Queen, 1998 CanLII 553 (TCC), [1998] 3 C.T.C. 2520, 98 DTC 1839:

items: Technical Risk or Uncertainty: Was there a technical risk or technological uncertainty that could not be removed by routine engineering or standard procedures?
Hypothesis Formulation: Did the person claiming to be doing SR&ED formulate hypotheses specifically aimed at reducing or eliminating that technological uncertainty?
Accordance with the Scientific Method: Did the procedures adopted accord with the total discipline of the scientific method, including formulating, testing, and modifying hypotheses?
Technological Advancement: Did the process result in a technological advance—that is, an advancement in general understanding?
Contemporaneous Record-Keeping: Did the taxpayer keep a detailed record of the hypotheses, tests, and results as the work progressed?

body.text: Appellate and Tax Court jurisprudence quickly reinforced how these five criteria interact in practice. In C.W. Agencies Inc. v. The Queen, 2001 FCA 393 (affirming 2000 DTC 2372 (TCC)), the Federal Court of Appeal adopted Justice Bowman's five Northwest Hydraulic criteria as binding appellate law, cited alongside RIS-Christie Ltd. v. The Queen, 99 DTC 5087 (FCA) in the CRA's Claim Review Manual for Research and Technology Advisors. In 116736 Canada Inc. v. The Queen (TCC, 1998), Justice Archambault observed that while the Income Tax Act and Regulations do not make written reports a strict statutory prerequisite where credible oral testimony proves SR&ED occurred, claimants without contemporaneous documentation face a heavy evidentiary burden—and CRA reviewers routinely deny undocumented claims. Conversely, as Justice D'Arcy held in the Jentel Tax Court appeal, even where a claimant maintains thorough records proving a systematic investigation, the claim fails if the evidence fails to establish genuine technological risk or technological advancement.
3.3 Modern Appellate Enforcement: Scientific Method, Guidelines, and Expert Evidence

Between 2021 and 2026, the Federal Court of Appeal forcefully rejected taxpayer attempts to bypass the Northwest Hydraulic framework by invoking CRA administrative guidelines or inadmissibly broad expert opinions. In Kam-Press Metal Products Ltd. v. Canada, 2021 FCA 88, the Federal Court of Appeal confirmed that the Northwest Hydraulic criteria represent the proper legal interpretation of subsection 248(1) and emphasized that courts—not CRA administrative guidelines—interpret the Income Tax Act.

One year later, in National R&D Inc. v. Canada, 2022 FCA 72 (affirming 2020 TCC 47), the Tax Court found that a software development claimant faced genuine technological uncertainty (Criterion 1) but failed the remaining Northwest Hydraulic criteria. Dismissing the taxpayer's further appeal, Justice Rennie of the Federal Court of Appeal held that the CRA's August 2021 SR&ED eligibility guidelines did not remove Criterion 3 (adherence to the scientific method, applied flexibly in a manner suitable for applied sciences and the claimant's business environment), upholding the denial because the taxpayer's records were "vague", "unclear", and failed to show a logical progression between experimental premise and result. Equally important, the Federal Court of Appeal upheld the exclusion of the taxpayer's expert report, warning that expert witnesses cannot opine directly on whether work legally constitutes SR&ED—an ultimate legal question reserved for the judge (contrasting an earlier trial ruling, 2021 TCC 27). Subsequent jurisprudence—including Manning Canning Kitchens Inc. v. His Majesty the King, 2024 TCC 159, and Tuna Temple, 2026 FCA 175—confirms the unbroken enforcement of all five Northwest Hydraulic criteria through 2026.

body.text: 4. Qualifying Expenditures (QREs) and Calculation Methodologies
4.1 Proxy Method vs. Traditional Method Election and Computing / Cloud Overhead

On Lines 160 and 162 of Form T661, a claimant selects either the Proxy Method (clause 37(8)(a)(ii)(B)) or the Traditional Method (clause 37(8)(a)(ii)(A) and ITR subsections 2900(2) and 2900(3)) to account for SR&ED overhead and support expenditures. Under the Proxy Method, the claimant avoids identifying, tracking, and allocating actual overhead expenses; instead, in Part 5 of Form T661, it computes a notional substitute amount—the Prescribed Proxy Amount (PPA)—equal to 55% (Line 820) of the salary base of employees directly engaged in SR&ED in Canada (subject to specified-employee caps and an overall cap). While the 55% PPA is excluded from the subsection 37(1) pool of deductible SR&ED expenditures, it enters qualified SR&ED expenditures to earn SR&ED ITCs.

Under the Traditional Method, no PPA is computed; instead, the claimant must specifically identify, track, allocate, explain, and substantiate actual overhead and other expenditures that are directly related and incremental to the prosecution of SR&ED (ITR paragraph 2900(2)(c))—meaning the outlay would not have been incurred had the SR&ED not taken place—or directly attributable to SR&ED premises, facilities, or equipment (ITR subsection 2900(3)). Traditional-method overhead enters both the subsection 37(1) deductible pool and the ITC qualified expenditure pool, benefiting shop-floor or utility-intensive claimants whose actual incremental overhead exceeds 55% of direct wages. Notably, no separate standalone "cloud computing" rule appears in the CRA's SR&ED policies: incremental software/computing expenses that would not have been incurred absent the SR&ED work are claimable only as substantiated incremental overhead under the traditional method (ITR paragraph 2900(2)(c)), whereas under the proxy method such overhead is absorbed within the 55% PPA (unless an outlay qualifies as an eligible post-December 15, 2024 equipment lease or depreciable hardware acquisition).

body.text: 4.2 Salaries, Wages, Specified Employee Caps, YMPE Limits, and Foreign Labour

Under subsection 248(1) and the CRA's SR&ED Salary or Wages Policy (updated January 28, 2025), allowable SR&ED salary or wages comprise gross employment remuneration (such as T4 wages) incurred for SR&ED performed in Canada, including cash outlays for taxable benefits (automobile benefits, housing/board/meals, tuition, group term life insurance) and reasonable actual costs of non-cash taxable benefits (excluding recoverable GST/HST or PST, provided the underlying cost is not also deducted as a business expense). For employees other than specified employees, bonuses and profit-based remuneration qualify as allowable SR&ED wages, though ITR subsection 2900(9) excludes all bonuses, profit-based pay, taxable benefits, and prior-year unpaid wages paid in the year from the PPA salary base. Conversely, SR&ED salary or wages strictly exclude the employer's share of related benefits, extended vacation or sick leave, stock option benefits, retiring allowances, and any remuneration not paid within 180 days after the end of the taxation year (subsection 78(4)).

Strict statutory caps govern specified employees (detailed in Section 6.0 of the SR&ED Salary or Wages Policy: employees who do not deal at arm's length with the employer or who are specified shareholders owning, directly or indirectly, 10% or more of the issued shares of any class of the capital stock of the employer or of any related corporation). First, under subsection 37(9), bonuses and remuneration based on profits for specified employees are excluded. Second, under subsection 37(9.1), a specified employee's maximum allowable SR&ED salary cannot exceed 5 times the Year's Maximum Pensionable Earnings (YMPE) determined under section 18 of the Canada Pension Plan for the calendar year in which the taxation year ends, prorated by the number of days in the year the individual is a specified employee. Where a specified employee is employed by two or more associated corporations, no SR&ED wages can be claimed unless every associated corporation files Form T1174 (with a certified copy of the authorizing directors' resolution, or signed sole-shareholder confirmation) allocating no more than 5 × YMPE across the group. Third, under ITR subsection 2900(7), inclusion of a specified employee's wages in the proxy salary base is restricted to the lesser of 75% of total base salary/wages (SR&ED and non-SR&ED combined, excluding bonuses, profit-based pay, taxable benefits, and prior-year unpaid wages) or 2.5 × YMPE × (Days Employed in Tax Year ÷ 365). Although Canada introduced a higher second CPP ceiling (YAMPE) in 2024, SR&ED specified-employee formulas remain anchored strictly to the first ceiling (YMPE).

body.text: Claimants may also claim "permissible salary or wages" for SR&ED performed outside Canada up to 10% of salaries and wages directly attributable to SR&ED carried on in Canada, provided five cumulative requirements are met: the work is performed directly by an employee (never a contractor); the employee was a resident of Canada when the expense was incurred; the work relates to a business of the claimant; the work outside Canada is an integral part and solely in support of an SR&ED project carried out in Canada; and the wages are not subject to income or profits tax from another country. Permissible foreign salaries do not enter the proxy salary base, which is restricted to SR&ED performed in Canada.
4.3 Materials Consumed or Transformed, Production Runs, Subcontracts, and Third-Party Payments

Under ITR paragraph 2900(2)(a) and the CRA's Materials for SR&ED Policy, claimants under both the proxy and traditional methods may claim 100% of the cost of materials consumed or materials transformed in the prosecution of SR&ED in Canada. Where experimental development overlaps with plant operations under the SR&ED During Production Runs Policy, all labour, overhead, and material costs attributable to commercial production or excess production are excluded, and if a resulting product is sold or converted to commercial use, ITC recapture (subsections 127(27)–(36)) applies to the allowable materials transformed in SR&ED.

External R&D expenditures divide into three distinct statutory categories. First, arm's length SR&ED contracts—where the payer controls the SR&ED work, holds exclusive rights to the work, deals with a taxable supplier performing the work in Canada, and accounts on an accrual basis (subject to the 180-day unpaid rule in subsection 127(26))—are 100% deductible under subsection 37(1) and 80% eligible as qualified expenditures for ITC purposes (never entering the 55% PPA salary base). Second, third-party payments—accounted for on a cash basis (or fair market value of property/services supplied) to approved universities, research institutes, or agricultural organizations (including agricultural check-off dues), where the performer controls basic or applied research, rights are generally non-exclusive, and the claimant gains a preferential right to exploit results related to its business—are likewise 80% eligible for ITCs. Third, non-arm's length (NAL) SR&ED contracts (section 251) enter the payer's subsection 37(1) deductible pool at 100% but earn 0% ITC for the payer (and do not reduce the NAL performer's qualified expenditures as a contract payment); instead, non-partnership NAL parties may jointly file Form T1146 (subsection 127(13), reported on Form T661 Line 540) to transfer qualified expenditures up to the least of the agreed amount, the performer's year-end qualified expenditure pool, and amounts paid within 180 days of the performer's year-end. Purchases of non-contract goods or services from NAL suppliers are capped under subsection 127(11.6) at the supplier's adjusted selling or service cost on Form T661 Lines 542 and 543.
4.4 Restored Capital Expenditures, Shared-Use Equipment, Lease Costs, and Pool Calculation

Enacted via Bill C-15, depreciable property acquired and available for use after December 15, 2024 and equipment lease costs first payable after December 15, 2024 once again qualify for SR&ED incentives (expenditures on property acquired before December 16, 2024 remain ineligible). Under paragraph 37(1)(b) and the SR&ED Capital Expenditures Policy (June 29, 2026), new or used depreciable property (excluding land and buildings) qualifies at 100% for both subsection 37(1) deduction and ITC calculation (with 40% refundability on 35% enhanced ITCs) if intended at acquisition to use all or substantially all (ASA — 90% or more) of its operating time over its expected useful life, or consume ASA (90% or more) of its value, in performing SR&ED in Canada.

Where post-December 15, 2024 depreciable property (other than Prescribed Depreciable Property) is used primarily (more than 50%, but less than 90%, of operating time) in SR&ED in Canada, it qualifies as Shared-Use Equipment (SUE) on Line 504 of Form T661 (with NAL s. 127(11.6) adjustments applied directly on Line 504) for ITC purposes only. SUE earns ITCs on up to 50% of its capital cost across two periods: 25% (First-Term SUE) at the end of the first taxation year finishing at least 12 months after acquisition, and 25% (Second-Term SUE) at the end of the first taxation year finishing at least 24 months after acquisition, while capital depreciation remains governed by CCA on Schedule T2SCH8 (with earned SUE ITCs reducing next year's CCA class UCC). Similarly, post-December 15, 2024 equipment lease costs used ASA (≥90%) qualify under both methods (excluding general-purpose office equipment or furniture under the proxy method), whereas equipment leased after December 15, 2024 and used less than 90% in SR&ED can be claimed pro rata on Line 360 as overhead under the traditional method (for straddle tax years beginning before December 16, 2024, operating-time percentages are measured strictly after December 15, 2024). Selling or converting SR&ED capital property or SUE to commercial use triggers ITC recapture on Schedule T2SCH31 or Form T2038(IND).

Under paragraph 37(1)(d) and subsection 127(18), all government assistance (including provincial/territorial R&D credits, except credits on pre-December 16, 2024 capital property excluded from Line 514), non-government assistance, and arm's length contract payments reduce qualified SR&ED expenditures (with NAL assistance allocable via Form T1145). Under the proxy method, the portion of a provincial R&D credit attributable to the 55% PPA does not reduce the subsection 37(1) deductible pool (being included directly in income under paragraph 12(1)(x) in the year received), but still reduces federal qualified expenditures for ITC purposes under subsection 127(18). Form T661 computes Total Qualified SR&ED Expenditures for ITC Purposes in six sequential steps:

items: Gather Allowable SR&ED Expenditures: Aggregate allowable direct SR&ED wages (including ≤10% foreign permissible wages), materials consumed/transformed, subcontracts, third-party payments, post-December 15, 2024 ASA capital and lease outlays, and (if traditional method) incremental overhead.

Determine Gross Qualified Expenditures: Sum 100% of direct current and ASA capital/lease outlays, 80% of arm's length contracts and third-party payments, 25%/25% SUE (Line 504), and the 55% PPA (if proxy method), less prescribed expenditures, NAL contracts, non-taxable supplier payments, NAL cost caps (s. 127(11.6)), unpaid amounts (s. 127(26)), and assistance/contract payments (s. 127(18)).
Determine SR&ED Qualified Expenditure Pool: Add qualified expenditures transferred from an NAL performer and subtract amounts transferred to an NAL payer via Form T1146 (s. 127(13)).
Add Repayments: Add current-year repayments of previously deducted assistance or contract payments (earning ITCs at the 15% or 35% rate applicable in the original year).
Exclude Exempt-Income Expenditures: Deduct expenditures tied to businesses earning income exempt from Part I tax.
Claim ITC: Carry the resulting total to Schedule T2SCH31 (corporations) or Form T2038(IND) (individuals).

body.text: 5. Provincial and Territorial R&D Tax Credit Regimes
5.1 Coast-to-Coast Overview and Dual Tax Administration

Nine provinces and Yukon provide sub-national R&D tax credits atop federal SR&ED, while Prince Edward Island, the Northwest Territories, and Nunavut offer no provincial or territorial R&D tax credit. Eight jurisdictions (British Columbia, Saskatchewan, Manitoba, Ontario, New Brunswick, Nova Scotia, Newfoundland and Labrador, and Yukon) are administered by the CRA via T2/T1 schedules, whereas Quebec (Revenu Québec, CO-17 return) and Alberta (Province of Alberta, AT1 return) administer independent provincial regimes.

body.text: 5.2 Quebec: The 2025–2026 CRIC Consolidation and Adjacent Innovation Regimes

Under Quebec's 2025–2026 fiscal reform (Quebec Finance Bulletin 2025-6), for taxation years or fiscal periods beginning after March 25, 2025, Quebec abolished six legacy tax measures—the R&D salaries and wages credit (which paid 14% base or 30% enhanced for taxation years beginning on or before March 25, 2025), the university/public research centre/consortium credit, the research consortium fees/dues credit, the private partnership pre-competitive research credit, the technological adaptation services credit, and the industrial design component of the design credits—replacing them with the unified Tax Credit for Research, Innovation and Commercialization (CRIC) (Crédit d'impôt pour la recherche, l'innovation et la commercialisation).

Claimed via Form RD-1029.8.CR-T (RD-1029.8.CR) attached to the CO-17 corporate return, CRIC provides a 100% refundable credit to all eligible corporations operating an establishment in Quebec regardless of corporate size or foreign ownership: 30% on the first $1,000,000 of qualified expenditures above the exclusion threshold (shared among associated corporations via Form RD-1029.8.EN, though corporate partners claiming through a partnership receive only 20%), and 20% on qualified expenditures exceeding $1,000,000. Beyond R&D, CRIC covers pre-commercialization activities performed in conjunction with Quebec R&D—specifically regulatory tests, technological validations, and studies for initial commercialization approval or certification, plus product design (form, aesthetics, improved functionality, and choice of materials)—alongside capital property acquisition costs (excluding land, buildings, or rights to use land/buildings). Qualified CRIC expenditures include 100% of Quebec R&D/pre-commercialization salaries, 50% of Quebec subcontracts, 50% of payments to eligible universities, public research centres, or consortia, and 100% of eligible capital property (net of assistance), to the extent the total exceeds an annual exclusion threshold equal to the greater of $50,000 (prorated for short years) or the sum of each employee's Quebec basic personal amount ($18,571 for 2025), prorated by time spent on eligible activities.

Pre-commercialization expenses that are not federal SR&ED appear only on the Quebec claim. For overlapping R&D outlays, although the CRA's Assistance and Contract Payments Policy text still lists the four abolished legacy Quebec credits and has not yet been updated to name CRIC, practitioners coordinate filings by entering the R&D portion of CRIC as government assistance reducing federal qualified expenditures under subsection 127(18). Quebec also prevents stacking multiple provincial credits on the same cost; as summarized by Canadian funding advisory sources, adjacent Quebec options include the CDAEIA (replacing the 30% IT-salary CDAE for fiscal years starting after December 31, 2025 for corporations significantly integrating artificial intelligence, paying 30% above an exclusion threshold—22% refundable + 8% non-refundable in 2026, 21% + 9% in 2027, and 20% + 10% from 2028—with an annual Investissement Québec certificate), the refundable 15% / 20% / 25% C3i hardware/equipment credit, and a preferential 2% Quebec corporate tax rate (down from 11.5%) deduction on income from commercializing qualifying IP in Quebec.
5.3 Ontario, Western Canada, Atlantic Provinces, Yukon, and Combined Stacking

In Ontario, corporations carrying on business through an Ontario permanent establishment under Part III of the Taxation Act, 2007 (Ontario) can access three CRA-administered credits. First, the 8% refundable Ontario Innovation Tax Credit (OITC) applies up to a $3,000,000 annual expenditure limit (including 100% of current expenditures and the 55% PPA), phasing out between $500,000 and $800,000 of prior-year group federal taxable income or $25,000,000 and $50,000,000 of prior-year specified paid-up capital. Second, the 20% refundable Ontario Business-Research Institute Tax Credit (OBRITC) (Schedule 568, Schedule 569, and Schedule 5 Line 470) applies up to $20,000,000 in annual cash contract outlays ($4,000,000 maximum credit across associated corporations) for Ontario SR&ED performed under Post-May 6, 1997 contracts with unconnected eligible Ontario universities, colleges, teaching hospital research institutes, the Ontario Centre of Innovation (formerly OCE), Networks of Centres of Excellence, or designated non-profits ("connected" includes >10% voting rights or >10% share FMV, partnership, or non-arm's length dealing), and small businesses can stack both the 20% OBRITC and 8% OITC. Third, the 3.5% non-refundable Ontario R&D Tax Credit (ORDTC) (Schedule T2SCH508) offsets Ontario corporate tax payable (carrying back 3 years and forward 20 years); a loss-stage company collects the refundable OITC plus federal SR&ED in cash (roughly 62% of direct proxy salaries) while parking the non-refundable 3.5% ORDTC until profitable.

Across Western, Atlantic, and Northern Canada, Alberta's Innovation Employment Grant (IEG) (AT1 Schedule 29 and Form AT4970) pays a 100% refundable 8% on Alberta R&D spending up to the corporation's two-year rolling average base and 20% on incremental spending above that base, capped at $4,000,000 annually. British Columbia (Form T666, $6,000,000 CCPC and ECPC refundable cap for tax years beginning after December 15, 2024) and Saskatchewan (T2SCH403, $1,000,000 CCPC refundable cap) each pay 10% (non-refundable above caps and for other corporations, carrying back 3 years and forward 10 years). Manitoba (T2SCH380) pays 15% uncapped (half refundable—7.5% cash / 7.5% non-refundable with 3-year back / 20-year forward carryover—for in-house R&D, and 100% refundable 15% for qualifying Manitoba institute contracts), while New Brunswick (T2SCH360), Nova Scotia (T2SCH340), Newfoundland and Labrador (T2SCH301 / T1129), and Yukon each pay 15% fully refundable (rising to 20% refundable in Yukon for payments to Yukon University).

Because provincial R&D credits reduce the federal qualified expenditure pool under subsection 127(18), combined cash recovery follows Provincial Credit + [35% × (Federal Qualified Pool − Provincial Credit)]. For example, in a Quebec coordination model from R&D Tax Academy, a CCPC incurring $1,200,000 in Quebec R&D salaries and $200,000 to a Quebec subcontractor ($100,000 at 50% = $1,300,000 gross CRIC base) with a $100,000 exclusion threshold has $1,200,000 of excess CRIC spending, earning $300,000 (30% on $1M) plus $40,000 (20% on $200k) = $340,000 refundable CRIC; deducting $340,000 from $2,000,000 of pre-assistance federal qualified expenditures leaves $1,660,000, earning $581,000 (35%) in federal SR&ED ITCs for $921,000 in combined cash. body.text: 6. Direct Innovation Grants, Clean Economy ITCs, and Federal Patent Box Status
6.1 Stacking Direct Grants with SR&ED: NRC IRAP and Government Assistance Rules

Alongside tax credits, Canadian SMEs frequently combine SR&ED with non-dilutive direct R&D contributions from the National Research Council of Canada Industrial Research Assistance Program (NRC IRAP), which provides technical advisory networks and targeted project funding—including over $135 million invested in October 2026 through DI Assist to help Canadian businesses develop defence and dual-use technologies, where 79% of supported firms employ fewer than 50 employees. Under paragraph 37(1)(d) and subsection 127(18), direct federal or provincial grants and subsidies received, entitled to be received, or reasonably expected to be received in respect of SR&ED reduce both the subsection 37(1) deductible pool and the subsection 127(9) qualified expenditure pool (with non-arm's length allocations governed by Form T1145, and specialized wage-subsidy rules documented in CRA guidance such as its Canada Emergency Wage Subsidy SR&ED policy). Because SR&ED continues to fund the unsubsidized portion of eligible R&D costs (plus eligible proxy overhead), combining direct grants with SR&ED lowers net out-of-pocket R&D cost substantially compared to claiming either program in isolation.
6.2 Enacted Clean Economy Investment Tax Credits and Federal Patent Box Status

Bill C-15 (Royal Assent March 26, 2026) also enacted significant expansions across Canada's Clean Economy Investment Tax Credits and capital depreciation rules. Specifically, Parliament extended full Carbon Capture, Utilization, and Storage (CCUS) ITC rates by five years through the end of 2035 (with lower phase-out rates applying from 2036 to 2040); expanded the Clean Technology Manufacturing ITC to cover antimony, indium, gallium, germanium, and scandium (for property acquired and available for use on or after November 4, 2025) as well as polymetallic extraction and processing; broadened the Clean Technology ITC to include waste biomass electricity/heat property and modified small nuclear energy property rules; enacted the Clean Electricity ITC (extending eligibility to the Canada Infrastructure Bank and Canada Growth Fund); and enacted immediate expensing for qualifying manufacturing and processing (M&P) buildings alongside the reinstated Accelerated Investment Incentive (AII). By contrast, the proposed "Productivity Mega Deduction" (which excludes Class 1 buildings) remained un-enacted proposed legislation as of September 2026.

Canada does not have a federal "patent box" tax regime as of November 2026: as reported by iPolitics on November 11, 2026, despite holding formal consultations in 2024 and including a patent box pledge in its 2025 federal election platform, the federal government omitted the measure across two consecutive subsequent budgets.
7. Governing Authorities, Filing Procedures, Pre-Claim Approval, and Audit Defence
7.1 Institutional Roles, Prescribed Forms, and Hard Statutory Deadlines

While Department of Finance Canada formulates R&D tax legislation, the Canada Revenue Agency (CRA) administers federal SR&ED (and eight sub-national regimes) through SR&ED Coordinating Tax Services Offices (CTSOs), deploying Research and Technology Advisors (RTAs) to review technical eligibility and Financial Reviewers (FRs) to audit expenditure calculations, supported by Guide T4088, the Self-Assessment and Learning Tool (SALT), the SR&ED Client Portal in My Business Account, and the First-Time Claimant Advisory Service.

Under subsection 37(11) and paragraph (m) of the definition of "investment tax credit" in subsection 127(9) (SR&ED Filing Requirements Policy), claimants must file Form T661 together with Schedule T2SCH31 (corporations) or Form T2038(IND) (individuals)—plus any required agreements (T2SCH49, T1145, T1146, T1174)—containing all prescribed information on or before the statutory SR&ED reporting deadline, fixed at 12 months after the income tax return filing due date:

items: Taxable Corporations (Paragraph 150(1)(a)): T2 return due 6 months after tax year-end; SR&ED reporting deadline is 18 months after the end of the taxation year (for a December 31, 2026 year-end, T2 is due June 30, 2027 and the absolute SR&ED deadline is June 30, 2028; tax-exempt corporations incurring SR&ED must file Form T661 by their 6-month return due date or face a penalty).
Individuals Carrying on Business (Subparagraph 150(1)(d)(ii)): T1 return due June 15 of the following year; SR&ED reporting deadline is 17.5 months after calendar year-end.
Trusts (Paragraph 150(1)(c) & Subsection 104(2)): T3 return due no later than 90 days after the trust's tax year-end; SR&ED reporting deadline is 12 months after that T3 due date.

body.text: Under subsection 37(11.1), the 18-month corporate reporting window is non-negotiable and non-extendable: filing a T2 early or late does not alter the deadline, missing prescribed fields can only be cured on or before the reporting deadline, and the reporting deadline continues to bind even during an active CRA review.
7.2 April 1, 2026 Pre-Claim Approval, AI Triage, Audit Records, and 50% Penalties

Effective April 1, 2026, the CRA launched its optional pre-claim approval process inside My Business Account, enabling eligible businesses to obtain a pre-claim technical eligibility determination from the CRA within eight weeks before starting R&D work or incurring costs, and cutting post-filing expenditure review processing targets in half—from 180 days to 90 days—alongside expanded artificial intelligence intake screening to spare low-risk claims from unnecessary audit interventions.

Where a claim is selected for audit, as summarized in SR&ED audit practice guidance, RTAs and FRs issue information requests (generally with 30-day response windows) for contemporaneous records backing Lines 270 to 282 of Part 2 of Form T661 and underlying cost ledgers, followed by a review meeting where oral explanations cannot substitute for dated experimental records, employee time tracking, contracts, and post-December 15, 2024 equipment operating-time logs. Claimants must also report complete claim preparer information in Part 9 of Form T661 (paragraph 37(11)(b)). Under subsection 163(2) (paragraph 163(2)(d)) and the CRA's Gross Negligence Penalty on Overstated SR&ED Claims Policy (January 28, 2025), knowingly or under circumstances of gross negligence making a false statement or omission on an SR&ED claim triggers a 50% civil penalty on the overstated reduction or refund (for example, $31,500 on an overstated $63,000 claim). Disputed audit findings may be escalated under the CRA's Guidelines for resolving claimants' SR&ED concerns and corporate dispute procedures, and appealed to the Tax Court of Canada and Federal Court of Appeal.
